raucous

RAW-kus -- from Latin raucus ('hoarse, harsh-sounding'). · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Raucous is making a harsh, loud noise; disorderly and boisterous.

The comedy club's Friday crowd was always the most raucous of the week, howling with laughter at every punchline.

Example

By midnight, the reunion had turned genuinely raucous, with three different conversations shouted over a blaring playlist.

That loud, disorderly, high-energy noise -- the kind that makes it hard to hear anything else -- is exactly what raucous describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

rowdy: Rowdy describes people and their behavior -- a rowdy table of fans shoving and joking. Raucous describes the sound itself: the harsh, disorderly noise such a crowd makes. A group can be rowdy while barely raising the volume; raucous is always loud.

grating: A grating sound is unpleasant because of its texture -- a fork scraping a plate is grating even at low volume. Raucous is bigger and wilder: loud, harsh, disorderly noise with real energy behind it, like a packed stadium in the final minute.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

hushed: very quiet and subdued

serene: peacefully calm and quiet

Where it sits · how overpowering the noise gets

boisterous → raucous → deafening

boisterous vs. raucous: Boisterous is milder than raucous: kids get boisterous after birthday cake, all racing and happy shrieks, while a raucous crowd is harsher and louder -- a roar that drowns out everything in the room.

deafening vs. raucous: Deafening is stronger than raucous: a raucous party is harsh and loud, but the demolition blast next door was deafening -- so loud it overwhelms the ears entirely, silencing the whole street for a moment.

Build the Word

The pieces

Put it together: Raucous traces back to Latin raucus, 'hoarse, harsh-sounding' -- but that root doesn't extend cleanly into other common modern English words, so raucous is best learned as a strong, standalone word for loud, disorderly noise.

Use the root in a new word: raucously: The whole bar cheered raucously the moment the underdog team scored.

Word Building

Word Choice

Raucous almost always describes sound -- a raucous crowd, a raucous party, a raucous laugh -- loud, disorderly, and full of energy, whether the tone is celebratory or simply chaotic.
